import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 447

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/447](https://www.erdosproblems.com/447)
- [Er65b] Erdős, Paul, *Some recent advances and current problems in number theory*. Lectures on
  Modern Mathematics, Vol. III (1965), 196-244.
- [Kl71] Kleitman, Daniel, *Collections of subsets containing no two sets and their union*.
  Proceedings of the LA Meeting AMS (1971), 153-155.
-/

open Filter

namespace Erdos447

/-- The largest size of a union-free collection $\mathcal{F}$ of subsets of $[n]$. -/
noncomputable def maxUnionFree (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  sSup { k | ∃ F : Finset (Finset (Fin n)), F.UnionFree ∧ F.card = k }

/--
How large can a union-free collection $\mathcal{F}$ of subsets of $[n]$ be? By union-free we mean
there are no solutions to $A\cup B=C$ with distinct $A,B,C\in \mathcal{F}$. Must
$\lvert \mathcal{F}\rvert =o(2^n)$?

In [Er65b] Erdős reported that the estimate $\lvert \mathcal{F}\rvert=o(2^n)$ was proved in
unpublished work by Sárközy and Szemerédi.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5]
theorem erdos_447.parts.i : answer(True) ↔
    (fun n : ℕ => (maxUnionFree n : ℝ)) =o[atTop] (fun n : ℕ => (2 : ℝ) ^ n) := by
  sorry

/--
How large can a union-free collection $\mathcal{F}$ of subsets of $[n]$ be? By union-free we mean
there are no solutions to $A\cup B=C$ with distinct $A,B,C\in \mathcal{F}$. Perhaps even
$$\lvert \mathcal{F}\rvert <(1+o(1))\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}?$$

Solved by Kleitman [Kl71], who proved
$$\lvert \mathcal{F}\rvert <(1+o(1))\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}.$$
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos447.lean"]
theorem erdos_447.parts.ii : answer(True) ↔
    ∃ c : ℕ → ℝ, (c =o[atTop] (1 : ℕ → ℝ)) ∧ ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop,
      (maxUnionFree n : ℝ) < (1 + c n) * (n.choose (n / 2) : ℝ) := by
  sorry

end Erdos447

reformulations.difference: Uses a natural-number supremum of attainable cardinalities rather than an explicit maximum over families.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For every n the set of attainable sizes contains 0 and is bounded above by 2^n. Its natural-number supremum is therefore attained and bounds every admissible family's cardinality. The scratch file proves attainment and equality with the finite maximum used by the linked proof. This remains valid at n = 0, where the maximum is 1.

reformulations.difference: Makes the source's strict (1+o(1)) upper bound explicit using an existential error sequence and the extremal size. The linked formal proof instead states asymptotic equivalence to the middle binomial coefficient.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Attainment of the maximum makes its upper bound equivalent to a uniform bound over all union-free families. Also, c =o[atTop] 1 means exactly c(n) → 0. Writing M(n) for the maximum and b(n) for the middle binomial coefficient, the middle layer is union-free, so M(n) ≥ b(n) > 0 for every n. The stated upper bound therefore squeezes M(n)/b(n) to 1. Conversely, if that ratio tends to 1, choosing c(n) = M(n)/b(n) - 1 + 1/(n+1) gives a vanishing error and the required strict inequality. Both equivalences were proved in the scratch file.

sources_consulted: Paul Erdős, Some recent advances and current problems in number theory (1965), relevant passage on pp. 228–229: https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1965-17.pdf
https://www.ams.org/pspum/019 (table of contents and chapter link)
review.notes: All three declarations were checked. Both answer(True) values and research solved tags agree with the source. /workspace/review/scratch.lean compiles successfully and verifies the forbidden-configuration definition, supremum semantics, uniform formulations of both parts, and the equivalence recorded above without relying on the problem's sorry theorems. Exhaustive evaluation gives maxima 1, 2, 3, 5, 9 for n = 0,…,4. Direct website requests encountered Cloudflare; relevant pages and the Erdős paper were read through r.jina.ai. The original Kleitman chapter required institutional/individual login, so its full text was unavailable. The linked formal proof has matching definitions and an equivalent final statement, with no explicit sorry or custom axioms; its Lean 4.29.1 certificate could not be independently reproduced under the installed Lean 4.33.1 because of compilation incompatibilities. These limitations do not leave the declarations' mathematical faithfulness unresolved. No repository files were modified.
